model_answer: Some regard the interview as a source of truth and, when done well, an art that reveals a person to the public. label: PYQ-style
stem: What was Rudyard Kipling's opinion of interviews, and what is ironic about it? (40–50 words)
hint: Immoral, crime, assault; Caroline's diary; interviewed Twain.
model_answer: Kipling condemned the interview outright as immoral, a crime and an assault on a person that deserved punishment; his wife Caroline recorded in 1892 how two reporters in Boston ruined their day. The irony is that Kipling had himself once interviewed Mark Twain, practising what he denounced.

label: PYQ-style
stem: 'The interview is both a supremely serviceable medium and an intrusion.' Discuss the views of the interview presented in Part I of 'The Interview'. (120–150 words)
hint: Age and reach → two camps → critics with phrases → paradox (Kipling, Wells) → Brian on power → balanced conclusion.
model_answer:
Christopher Silvester notes that the interview, invented about 130 years ago, has become a commonplace of journalism, and that opinions about it are sharply divided.

To its defenders it is a source of truth and, in skilled hands, an art. Denis Brian points out that almost everything we know of our contemporaries reaches us through one person asking questions of another, which gives the interviewer unprecedented power and influence. Silvester himself calls it a supremely serviceable medium of communication.

Its victims disagree. Naipaul felt interviews wound people and take away part of themselves; Lewis Carroll had a horror of interviewers and never consented; Kipling called the practice immoral, a crime and an assault; Wells spoke of an ordeal; Saul Bellow felt thumbprints on his windpipe. Yet Kipling interviewed Mark Twain and Wells interviewed Stalin, which shows how indispensable the form has become.

The interview intrudes, but it is also how the public comes to know the minds of its most interesting people.

scheme.step: Case for: truth, art, Brian's point, serviceable medium
Case against with at least three named critics and their phrases
Paradox and balanced conclusion; expression and length

label: PYQ-style
stem: What impression of Umberto Eco do you form from his interview with Mukund Padmanabhan? (120–150 words)
hint: Prolific and disciplined (interstices) → unified interests → narrative scholar → modest about identity (academic first) → humble about success → playful, vivid speaker.
model_answer:
Eco comes across as a man of enormous energy and quiet discipline. He has written more than forty scholarly works, five novels, children's books and columns, yet he explains it simply: he works in the interstices, the empty moments of the day, such as the time a visitor spends coming up in the lift. He does not feel scattered, because the same philosophical and ethical interests run through everything he writes.

He is an original thinker who learnt at twenty-two that scholarship could be told as a story, and he has written that way since, turning to novels at fifty almost by accident. He is modest about his fame: he calls himself a university professor who writes novels at the weekend, prefers academic conferences to writers' clubs, and treats the huge success of The Name of the Rose as a mystery, crediting timing and readers who enjoy difficulty rather than his own genius.

Above all, he is a delightful talker, explaining ideas with playful images.

scheme.step: Unified interests; narrative scholarship; novels at fifty
Modesty: academic first; mystery of the novel's success
